extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, policymakers, trade practitioners, and scholars interested in Canadian anti-dumping law and Tribunal procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical guidance on legal and procedural standards used by the Canadian Anti-dumping Tribunal (definitions, evidentiary tests, processes for preliminary determinations, and organisational/practical considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal link between dumping and material injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal must establish a relationship between dumping and material injury; if the relationship cannot be established, it is unclear to decide that dumping has created even an indeterminate degree of injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof ordinarily lies with the complainant; shifting to a negative test (requiring exporters/importers to disprove other causes) is inconsistent with Article VI of GATT and the Code. The Tribunal should make "a conscientious and careful effort to establish a judgment of reasonable confidence"; until the causal relationship is adequately explored, statements of reasons are vulnerable to being described as "mere allegations or hypothetical possibilities" (Article 3(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Other factors" (Article 3 of the Code) must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal must consider factors other than dumping that may adversely affect industry performance (e.g., recession, market saturation, intra-domestic competition, failure to keep abreast of product development, wage levels, changing employment patterns, higher cost materials, limited market size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons should reflect full exploration of alternative explanations; examples include Colour television (recession, saturation, competition) and Ladies' handbags (wage levels, materials, market size). Tribunal must decide whether other factors are solely responsible or merely increased susceptibility to injury from dumping ('thin skull' issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof: "judgment of reasonable confidence"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal does not require 'formal proof in the sense understood by a trial judge' but seeks 'a judgment of reasonable confidence' to establish causal relationships and injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase is used to lower the proof standard from judicial proof, but its exact meaning is uncertain and the Tribunal must still make a conscientious and careful effort to reach a reasoned conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding of "likelihood" of future injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal may find no past or present injury but a likelihood of future injury caused by continued dumping; this finding can extend beyond goods already dumped or contracted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is debate whether 'likelihood' may be found absent past/present injury and whether predictions can be based on the 'period under review' especially when no injury was found during that period (see Hydraulic turbines case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'domestic industry' / meaning of 'major proportion'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'domestic industry' refers to domestic producers as a whole of the like products or to those whose collective output constitutes a 'major proportion' of total domestic production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code negotiators may have thought 'major proportion' meant at least half, but Canadian practice treats 'major' as 'significant' not necessarily >50%; a producer or group representing less than 50% may still constitute a 'major proportion' — the question is one of degree and fact (endorsed by Federal Court of Appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of 'separate industry' (regional markets)
rubrics_metrics.description: A country may be divided into two or more competitive markets and producers within each market regarded as a separate industry where, because of transport costs or special regional marketing conditions, regional isolation exists (Article 4(a)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal has found separate industries in some geographic slices (e.g., wallboard west of a border) and rejected them in others. Article 8(e) restricts anti-dumping duties to products consigned for final consumption to that area, but subsection 16(4) of the Canadian Act references only Article 4, producing an anomaly: Canada apparently cannot levy 'regional' duties, allowing Canada-wide duties to protect regional industries — a legislative anomaly warranting change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'like goods' (identical or closely resemble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like goods are (a) goods identical in all respects to the said goods, or (b) in the absence of identical goods, goods the characteristics of which closely resemble those of the said goods (paragraph 2(1) of the Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is a mechanical characteristic comparison rather than a pure competition/substitutability test; where identical goods exist, goods that 'closely resemble' are excluded. Substitutability, functional similarity, or competitiveness alone do not meet the 'closely resemble' requirement; Tribunal must consider the totality of characteristics (physical characteristics, end use, market served). Cases: Metal storage/parts cabinets, Footwear, Preserved mushrooms, Steam traps, Sarco Canada.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deputy Minister's formulation of the class of goods is final for preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy Minister formulates the class of goods in a preliminary determination and that formulation is not subject to review by the Tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very narrow/detailed formulation by the Deputy Minister can effectively prevent the Tribunal from finding Canadian producers that have suffered injury; this formulation affects the difficulty of finding identical or closely resembling goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to treat components included in preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If the preliminary determination includes components or parts, each component is not necessarily treated as a separate article of commerce; components mainly assembled into finished goods may be treated with the finished article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal held components not to be treated separately where dumped components were assembled into finished zippers or where simple assembly feasibility demonstrated (Bicycles). General rule: where dumping of an article causes injury, continued dumping of major components will also likely cause injury — applied to avoid frustration of anti-dumping measures. Uncertainty remains if components are both separate articles of commerce and easily assembled, and whether component production in Canada is required before treating dumped components as 'like goods'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material injury indicators (use of Code's well-accepted indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material injury indicators adopted are those well-accepted and described by the Code; the Tribunal's indicators have been formalized by Rules of Procedure and are consistently applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While indicators themselves are well handled, the critical problem is relating indicated material injury to the dumping of like goods — the causal link is difficult and often inadequately explored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial inquiry and timelines for preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: After a formal complaint or initial inquiry, Special Assessment Programs will normally carry out initial inquiries within thirty days and, if evidence of dumping and injury exist, initiate a formal investigation normally to be completed within six months (1977 guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial inquiries include sending manufacturer's questionnaires and possible plant visits; formal investigation notice is sent to exporters/importers/government and published in Canada Gazette; timelines (about seven months to a preliminary determination) may burden domestic producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal complaint content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal complaint must identify the precise nature of the product, list the Canadian producers, give an estimate of the Canadian market, offer prima facie evidence of dumping (including countries of origin), and give prima facie evidence of material injury or retardation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manufacturer's questionnaire requires full description of goods, exporters/importers, unit selling prices, landed Canada prices, evidence of subsidies/rebates, and financial/production/sales/inventory/capacity/employment data — effectively comprehensive details of the formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaires, information gathering and verification practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Importers receive questionnaires to determine export transaction facts; exporters receive 'Request for Information' (sometimes preceded by preliminary queries); National Revenue may carry out overseas 'verification' of exporters' supplied information by undisclosed procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish normal value, foreign domestic sales are examined for an appropriate period (generally at least a 60-day period preceding sales to Canada); entries into Canada examined typically over a six-month period — together constituting the 'period under review' for preliminary determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate methods for normal value when information is insufficient or state-controlled economies involved
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Deputy Minister cannot gather sufficient information to determine normal or export price, or if goods are exported from a state-controlled economy, he may use section 11 or subsection 9(7) of the Act to prescribe another method of determination (e.g., based on value for another exporter of the same goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue Canada's practice is to issue a ministerial prescription in every case as a 'stand-by' to cover new models or new exporters not part of the original investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of provisional duties and provisional entry of dumped goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a preliminary determination that both dumping (not negligible) and some evidence of material injury exist, the Deputy Minister assesses provisional duties equal to the margin of dumping; importers either pay provisional duty or post security equal to that amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dumped goods subject to the preliminary determination imported into Canada between the preliminary determination date and the Tribunal's order/finding are entered provisionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of burdens and fairness concerns in the preliminary system
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic producers generally bear the burden of initiating the anti-dumping process and supplying much necessary information; producers normally wait about seven months before a preliminary determination and must often have resources to initiate proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a free trade perspective this high burden is defensible because anti-dumping measures are exceptional and should not be automatic; but there are practical concerns whether all producers have required resources and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Tribunal jurisdiction and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal has limited jurisdiction in certain statutory matters (e.g., cannot change the Deputy Minister's class formulation) but exercises significant discretion in areas like defining domestic industry and components, generally exercising it reasonably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite reasonable exercise of discretion in some areas, the Tribunal's record lacks obvious consistent criteria for judgment in certain respects; where discretion exists it has usually been used sensibly, but some statutory anomalies (e.g., inability to levy regional duties) and failures to fully explore causation remain.
